Central Solar Eclipses: 1991 - 2050

The following table provides links to maps and path coordinates for every central solar eclipse from 1991 through 2050. A central eclipse is one where the axis of the Moon's shadow intersects Earth's surface. It may be total, annular or hybrid (combination of both total and annular).

The global maps use an orthographic projection of Earth which shows the region of visibility for each eclipse. The path of the Moon's penumbral shadow (magenta and cyan) covers the region of partial eclipse, while the course to the umbral (blue) or antumbral (red) shadow defines the path of total or annular eclipse, respectively. These figures are described in greater detail in the Key to Solar Eclipse Maps. Each figure is stored as a GIF file of about 60 kilobytes.

The path tables include the geographic coordinates of the northern and southern limits, as well as the central line. The path characteristics are generated at 1 minute intervals of time compared to the 6 minute interval used in Fifty Year Canon of Solar Eclipses: 1986 - 2035. This should provide enough detail for making preliminary plots of the path on larger scale maps. Local circumstances on the central line include the Sun's altitide and azimuth, the path width (kilometers) and the duration of the central eclipse.

[1] Eclipse magnitude is the fraction of the Sun's diameter obscured by the Moon. For annular eclipses, the eclipse magnitude is always less than 1. For total eclipses, the eclipse magnitude is always greater than or equal to 1. For both annular and total eclipses, the value listed is actually the ratio of diameters between the Moon and the Sun.

[2] Central Duration is the duration of a total or annular eclipse at Greatest Eclipse. Greatest Eclipse is the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center.

[3] Hybrid eclipses are also known as annular/total eclipses. Such an eclipse is both total and annular along different sections of its umbral path.
